qs.q: Which of the following statements describes Computer Architecture?

c.x: The operational units and their interconnections that realize the specification
The attributes visible to the programmer that directly affect logical program execution
The hardware technology details that are chosen after the design is fixed
The performance characteristics revealed by how the units are connected

qs.e: Computer Architecture is the set of attributes visible to the programmer (instruction set, data-type sizes, I/O mechanisms, memory addressing) that directly affect the logical execution of a program. Option 1 describes Organization. Answer: attributes visible to the programmer.

qs.q: Which of the following is an architectural attribute (not an organizational one)?

c.x: The physical layout of the chips inside the processor
The speed at which a given processor model runs instructions
The hardware circuits that realize the control unit
The memory addressing techniques supported by the machine

qs.e: Architecture attributes are: instruction set, number of bits used to represent data types, I/O mechanisms, and memory addressing techniques. The other options describe how the architecture is realized (organization) and its performance. Answer: memory addressing techniques.

qs.q: Two processors of the Intel x86 family run exactly the same programs, but their internal designs and speeds are different. What does this show?

c.x: The architecture can change while the organization stays the same
Both the architecture and the organization must change in every new model
The organization can change while the architecture stays the same
The organization is fixed first and the architecture is decided afterwards

qs.e: All Intel x86 processors share the same basic architecture (programs run unchanged), yet their organization differs. Organization is decided after the architecture is fixed, so it can be changed without changing the architecture. Answer: organization changes, architecture stays.

qs.q: Which row correctly compares Computer Architecture with Computer Organization?

c.x: Architecture describes what the computer does; Organization describes how it does it
Architecture describes how the computer does it; Organization describes what it does
Architecture is decided after the organization; Organization is fixed first
Architecture reveals computer performance; Organization indicates computer hardware

qs.e: Architecture = the programmer's abstract view (what the computer does), fixed first and indicating the hardware. Organization = the realization of that architecture (how it does it), decided after the architecture and revealing performance. Answer: option 1.

qs.q: In his 1945 report First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC, Von Neumann organized the computer system into which four main parts?

c.x: Central processing unit, cache memory, main memory, and system buses
Central control unit, register file, memory, and input/output buses
Central arithmetical unit, central control unit, memory, and input/output devices
Central arithmetical unit, accumulator, memory, and bus controller

qs.e: The four parts are the Central Arithmetical unit (CA), the Central Control unit (CU), Memory (M), and Input/Output devices (I/O). Answer: CA, CU, Memory, I/O.

qs.q: Why can the IAS machine be called the father of all modern computers?

c.x: It was among the first computers to store both program and data in memory
It was the first computer to take its input and output on punch cards
It was the first computer to replace vacuum tubes with transistors
It was the first computer built entirely from integrated circuits on chips

qs.e: IAS was one of the first computers that kept both the program and the data in the computer's memory (the stored-program concept), and it was the prototype for the IBM family of computers. Answer: it stored program and data in memory.

qs.q: Why did Von Neumann leave the ENIAC design team and take part in developing the EDVAC?

c.x: He wanted a larger electronic memory for storing tabular functions and constants
He wanted to follow the engineering view of the creators rather than the logical view
He wanted to replace punch-card input and output with a direct keyboard interface
His interest was the logical structure, unlike the engineering view of ENIAC's creators

qs.e: Von Neumann's main interest was the logical structure and mathematical description of the new technology, while the ENIAC creators had an engineering view. This difference in point of view motivated him to leave ENIAC and join EDVAC. Answer: option 4.

qs.q: Which IAS register contains the address of the <u>next instruction pair</u> to be fetched from memory?

c.x: Memory Address Register (MAR)
Instruction Register (IR)
Instruction Buffer Register (IBR)
Program Counter (PC)

qs.e: The PC holds the address of the next instruction pair to be fetched. The MAR holds the address of the word being read or written, the IR holds the 8-bit opcode being executed, and the IBR holds the right-hand instruction temporarily. Answer: PC.

qs.q: A word fetched from memory contains two instructions. Which register is employed to hold the <u>right-hand</u> instruction temporarily while the left-hand instruction is executed?

c.x: Memory Buffer Register (MBR)
Instruction Buffer Register (IBR)
Instruction Register (IR)
Multiplier Quotient (MQ)

qs.e: The IBR temporarily holds the right-hand instruction of a word. Later, its opcode moves to the IR and its address field moves to the MAR, so no new memory access is needed. Answer: IBR.

qs.q: An IAS memory word has 40 bits. Each instruction is 20 bits and contains an 8-bit opcode. How many instructions are stored in one word, and how many bits are in the address field of one instruction?

c.x: 2 instructions per word; 12-bit address field
2 instructions per word; 8-bit address field
1 instruction per word; 12-bit address field
4 instructions per word; 12-bit address field

e: Instructions per word = word size / instruction size = $40 / 20 = 2$ (a left-hand and a right-hand instruction).

qs.q: The CPU must write a word into memory location 100. Which register roles are used for this transfer?

c.x: The PC holds the address and the IBR holds the word
The MBR holds the address and the MAR holds the word
The MAR holds the address and the MBR holds the word
The IR holds the address and the AC holds the word

qs.e: The MAR specifies the address in memory of the word to be written or read, and the MBR contains the word to be stored in memory (or the word received from memory). Answer: MAR = address, MBR = data.

qs.q: The IAS Selectron memory has up to 1024 words, and each word is 40 bits. What is the total memory capacity in bits?

c.x: 40,960 bits
20,480 bits
81,920 bits
4,096 bits

e: Number of words = $1024$, each word has $40$ bits.
(Check: $20480$ would use 20-bit words, which is the size of one <u>instruction</u>, not a word.)

qs.q: A program is resident in RAM and is about to start running. Which register must be initialized first, and with what?

c.x: The IR, with the opcode of the first instruction
The MAR, with the size of the program in words
The PC, with the address of the first instruction
The AC, with the value of the first operand

qs.e: The fetch-execute cycle starts with `MAR ← PC`, so the PC must already hold the address of the first instruction of the program. The IR, MAR and MBR are then filled automatically by the fetch step. Answer: PC = address of the first instruction.
